question.text: Electrons with energy <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>80</mn><mo> </mo><mi>keV</mi></math> are incident on the tungsten target of an X-ray tube. K-shell electrons of tungsten have <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>72</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>5</mn><mo> </mo><mi>keV</mi></math> energy. X-rays emitted by the tube contain only

options.text: A continuous X-ray spectrum (Bremsstrahlung) with a minimum wavelength of  0.155 Å
A continuous X-ray spectrum (Bremsstrahlung) with all wavelengths
The characteristic X-ray spectrum of tungsten
A continuous X-ray spectrum (Bremsstrahlung) with a minimum wavelength of0.155 Å and the characteristic X-ray spectrum of tungsten

solution.text:
Minimum wavelength of continuous X - ray spectrum is given

by λ min (in Å) = 12375E

Here E = energy of incident electrons (in eV) = energy corresponding to minimum wavelength

E = 80 keV = 80 x 103 eV

Therefore, λmin (ni Å)= 1237580×103=0.155

Also, the energy of the incident electrons (80 keV) is more than the ionization energy of the K - shell electrons (i. e., 72. 5 keV), Therefore, characteristic X-ray spectrum will also be obtained because the energy of the incident electron is high enough to knock out the electron from K or L- shells.
